acts.note.120:1.desc: On Salvington, Michael's brother-trustee commissioned him for his seventh and final bestowal. This time Michael would appear on Urantia as a helpless babe, wholly subject to his Father's will, while his brother assumed jurisdiction of the universe and pledged that no rebellion could occur during his absence.
acts.note.120:2.desc: His brother set out nine counsels for the bestowal: grow up as a child of Urantia, technically end the Lucifer rebellion as the Son of Man, function largely as a teacher, pour out the Spirit of Truth, and reveal the Father. He cautioned Michael to refrain from any superhuman will-to-power after his Thought Adjuster arrived.
acts.note.120:3.desc: After consulting with Gabriel, the brother added supplementary advice: follow the accepted family customs of the day, avoid entanglement in economic and political matters, found no sect, leave no writings or likenesses, and probably not marry. Then, in the presence of all Salvington assembled, Michael removed himself from their midst.
acts.note.120:4.desc: Christ Michael was truly a dual-origin being, but not a double personality; he was God incarnate in man. He did not progressively become God, for Jesus was always God and man. The supreme spiritual purpose of the bestowal was to enhance the revelation of God.
acts.note.121:1.desc: When Jesus was born, the world offered the most favorable conditions for a Creator Son's bestowal. Roman political systems, Greek language and culture, and Jewish religious and moral teachings unified the Occident, while good roads and seas cleared of pirates made travel and trade flourish.
acts.note.121:2.desc: The Jews, the most influential group of the Semitic peoples, lived in Palestine, the crossroads of three continents. Their more than two hundred synagogues across the Roman world became bases for the new gospel, and under Herod the Idumean and later his son Herod Antipas the Jews longed for a Messiah.
acts.note.121:3.desc: First-century Mediterranean society was divided into five classes: the aristocracy, the business groups, the small middle class, the free proletariat, and the slaves. Half the population of the Roman state were slaves, yet there was little class consciousness, and Christianity was not an economic movement.
acts.note.121:4.desc: The gentile world was dominated by four philosophies derived from Platonism: the Epicurean, the Stoic, the Cynic, and the Skeptic. Stoicism reached a lofty morality but did not know God as a Father, while the Cynics, preserving remnants of Melchizedek's teachings, helped prepare the common people for the later Christian missionaries.
acts.note.121:5.desc: The religions of the Occident included the pagan cults, emperor worship, astrology, and the mystery religions. The mysteries, with their promise of personal salvation, prepared the way for Jesus' teachings to spread, yet Paul's Christianity surpassed them by resting on moral redemption and on a historic fact.
acts.note.121:6.desc: Jerusalem's religious thought had been strongly influenced by Greek culture and philosophy, aided greatly by the Greek translation of the Hebrew scriptures. Philo of Alexandria harmonized Greek philosophy with Hebrew theology, and Paul made use of this harmonization as a foundation for his Christian cult.
acts.note.121:7.desc: Bound by law and tradition, the Jews would not share Yahweh with the gentiles and so failed to become messengers of the new gospel. Religious evolution passed westward to Europe, and Paul's Antioch Christianity blended Jesus' gospel with Greek philosophy, mystery-cult teachings, and Jewish morality.
acts.note.121:8.desc: The midwayer author explains that he drew on the lost notes of Andrew and on the four Gospels. Mark wrote from Peter's memories, completing his Gospel in A.D. 68; Isador wrote Matthew's at Pella in 71; Luke wrote in Achaia in 82; and Nathan began John's Gospel in 101 at John's urging.
acts.note.122:1.desc: Joseph came from a line of skilled mechanics, and David and Solomon were not in his direct ancestry. Mary's varied lineage included remarkable women such as Tamar, Ruth, and Bathsheba. Gabriel chose this ideal yet ordinary couple as the bestowal parents.
acts.note.122:2.desc: Late in June, 8 B.C., Gabriel appeared to Elizabeth at noontide and announced that she would bear John, the forerunner of a divine teacher. For five months she told no one, not even her husband, and Zacharias, long skeptical, was fully convinced by a dream only about six weeks before John's birth.
acts.note.122:2.diff: The Gospel of Luke says an angel appeared to Zacharias as he burned incense in the temple and struck him mute for his unbelief, whereas The Urantia Book says Gabriel appeared to Elizabeth and Zacharias was later convinced by a dream.
acts.sub.122:2.6: Mary visits Elizabeth in the city of Judah
acts.note.sub:122:2.6.desc: Gabriel appeared to Mary about the middle of November, 8 B.C. Later, with Joseph's consent, Mary journeyed to the City of Judah, four miles west of Jerusalem in the hills, to visit Elizabeth. She stayed three weeks as they compared experiences, and Elizabeth did much to strengthen Mary's faith.
acts.note.sub:122:2.6.diff: The Gospel of Luke says Mary stayed about three months, the babe leaped in Elizabeth's womb, and Mary sang a hymn of praise, whereas The Urantia Book says only that she stayed three weeks while the two women compared experiences.
acts.note.sub:122:2.7.desc: John was born in the City of Judah on March 25, 7 B.C. Zacharias and Elizabeth rejoiced greatly, and at his circumcision on the eighth day they named him John, as they had been directed. A nephew of Zacharias had already set out for Nazareth to carry the news to Mary.
acts.note.sub:122:2.7.diff: The Gospel of Luke says Zacharias wrote the name John on a tablet, regained his speech, and prophesied, whereas The Urantia Book mentions neither his being struck mute nor any prophecy.
acts.note.122:3.desc: One evening about sundown, the day after Mary conceived, Gabriel appeared to her in her Nazareth home and announced that she would bear a son named Joshua, who would inaugurate the kingdom of heaven. Mary told Joseph only weeks later, and after much pondering he concluded that they had been chosen as parents of the Messiah.
acts.note.122:3.diff: The Gospel of Luke says a virgin would conceive by the Holy Spirit and the child would receive the throne of David, whereas The Urantia Book places the announcement the day after Mary had already conceived and mentions no throne of David.
acts.note.122:4.desc: Joseph was reconciled only after a dream in which a celestial messenger told him that in Mary's son would be life, and his life would become the light of mankind. Joseph was not of David's line; an orphaned ancestor had been adopted by Zadoc, a descendant of David. Many Messianic prophecies were applied to Jesus long afterward.
acts.note.122:4.diff: The Gospel of Matthew says an angel told Joseph, son of David, of a conception by the Holy Spirit fulfilling the virgin prophecy, whereas The Urantia Book says nothing was said about David's house and that "a maiden" was later changed to "a virgin."
acts.map6.head: Old Nazareth and the Home of Jesus
acts.map6.sub: 4 B.C. – about A.D. 28  ·  Papers 122–150  ·  location sketch
acts.map6.1.head: The home of Jesus
acts.map6.1.body: A one-room stone house with a flat roof, built by Joseph with the help of two of his brothers, with an adjoining building for the animals and, in the back yard, the shelter for the oven and mill. Mary kept a dovecote on top of the animal house. As a boy he played with John in the sand on top of the house. It stood on the outskirts, about midway between the base of the hill and the road to Cana.
acts.map6.2.head: The village spring
acts.map6.2.body: The spring in the eastern section of the town, a center of contact and gossip for the entire town. Before he was eight he had talked there with the mothers and young women of Nazareth, and he befriended Nathan, the potter who worked near the spring.
acts.map6.3.head: The caravan repair shop
acts.map6.3.body: The small workshop Joseph built in midsummer, 3 B.C., close to the village spring and near the caravan tarrying lot. Here Jesus listened to caravan travelers from the four corners of the earth. In A.D. 12 he began buying it back and worked there; children gathered by the shop to hear his stories.
acts.map6.4.head: The synagogue
acts.map6.4.body: As a young man he often spoke here, and the manuscript later handed to him was one he had presented to it. Years later, after he spoke in this synagogue, a mob rushed him out to the brow of a near-by precipitous hill.
acts.map6.5.head: The hill of Simeon
acts.map6.5.body: The high hill in the northerly part of Nazareth, among the highest of southern Galilee. From the summer of his fourteenth year he often climbed it for prayer and meditation; in his prayer on the hilltop he declared himself ever subject to the will of his Paradise Father.
acts.map6.6.head: The family garden
acts.map6.6.body: About his fifteenth year he rented land just to the north of the home and divided it into family garden plots, which he worked with his younger brothers and sisters. His favorite stroll was the narrow trail winding northeast about the base of the hill to the road to Sepphoris.
acts.map2.head: Nazareth and Its Surroundings in Childhood
acts.map2.1.head: The home in Nazareth
acts.map2.1.body: A one-room stone house built by Joseph with the help of two of his brothers. It stood on the outskirts, not far from the high hill in the northerly part of the town, a little south and east of the hill's southern promontory, toward the road to Cana, and some distance from the village spring.
acts.map2.2.head: The hill of Simeon
acts.map2.2.body: The hill to the northwest of Nazareth. In the summer of his fourteenth year he often climbed it for prayer and meditation. From the summit he looked upon Megiddo, Taanach, the hills of Dothan, and Ebal and Gerizim, recalling the history of his father's people (dotted lines). Save the Mount Tabor range to the east and the hill of Nain, it was the highest hill of southern Galilee.
acts.map2.3.head: Uncle's farm
acts.map2.3.body: Country home of his mother's brother, on the Megiddo road near Sarid, several miles south of Nazareth. Fleeing an epidemic in July 3 B.C., they stayed there more than two months, his first experience on a farm; he often visited it later.
acts.map2.4.head: Fisherman uncle at Magdala
acts.map2.4.body: Excused from school one week each month for his good work, he often spent it with his fisherman uncle on the shores of the Sea of Galilee near Magdala. The route is not given in the text (dashed).
acts.note.122:5.desc: Joseph was quiet, reflective, and held the Eastern, or Babylonian, views of the Jewish religion; Mary was cheerful, practical, and leaned toward the broader Hellenistic interpretation. They married at Mary's home near Nazareth when Joseph was twenty-one, and Jesus inherited his father's gentleness and his mother's gift as a teacher.
acts.note.122:6.desc: The home of Jesus stood near the high hill in the northern part of Nazareth, at the edge of the village. It was a one-room stone house with a flat roof, furnished with a low stone table, a loom, and a mill and oven in the back yard. After Martha's birth Joseph added a large room for a workshop and bedroom.
acts.map1.head: The Birth of Jesus and the Flight to Egypt
acts.map1.1.head: From Nazareth to Bethlehem
acts.map1.1.body: August 18–20, 7 B.C. The journey to enroll for the census. Around the foothills of Mount Gilboa, the first night by the river Jordan; past the foot of Mount Sartaba to Jericho for the second night; then by Jerusalem to Bethlehem.
acts.map1.2.head: Flight to Alexandria in Egypt
acts.map1.2.body: Mid-October, 6 B.C., the night before the massacre of the infants. They journeyed alone; the route is not given in the text (dashed).
acts.map1.3.head: Back to Joppa by boat
acts.map1.3.body: Late August, 4 B.C., on their friend Ezraeon's boat. They went directly to Bethlehem and spent the entire month of September there.
acts.map1.4.head: Return to Nazareth
acts.map1.4.body: Early October, 4 B.C., by way of Lydda and Scythopolis, arriving on the fourth day.
acts.note.122:7.desc: Augustus' census was taken in Herod's kingdom a year late, in 7 B.C. Despite Joseph's objections Mary insisted on going, and they left Nazareth on August 18, traveling by the Jordan valley and Jericho. Reaching Bethlehem on August 20, they lodged in a grain storage room of the rock-hewn stables below the inn.
acts.note.122:7.diff: The Gospel of Luke says Joseph went to be enrolled because he was of David's house, whereas The Urantia Book says Mary did not need to go but chose to accompany him, and that the census was delayed a year by Herod's troubles.
acts.note.122:8.desc: At noon on August 21, 7 B.C., in the stable lodging at Bethlehem, Mary gave birth to Jesus with the help of women fellow travelers and laid him in a manger. The next day Joseph enrolled and the family moved up to the inn; at the wish of Zacharias and Elizabeth they stayed in Bethlehem more than a year.
acts.note.122:8.diff: The Gospel of Luke says only that the babe was laid in a manger because there was no room at the inn, whereas The Urantia Book gives the date and noon hour, the move to the inn the next day, and a stay of over a year.
acts.sub.122:8.2: Circumcision and naming on the eighth day
acts.note.sub:122:8.2.desc: The promised child was born in Bethlehem in just the same manner as all babies before and since. On the eighth day he was circumcised according to Jewish practice and was formally named Joshua (Jesus).
acts.sub.122:8.5: The seraphim sing over the manger
acts.note.sub:122:8.5.desc: At the noontide birth of Jesus, the seraphim of Urantia sang anthems of glory over the Bethlehem manger, but their songs were not heard by human ears. No shepherds or other mortal creatures came to pay homage to the babe until the priests from Ur arrived.
acts.note.sub:122:8.5.diff: The Gospel of Luke says angels and a heavenly host appeared to shepherds by night and the shepherds came to see the child, whereas The Urantia Book says the seraphic anthems went unheard and no shepherds came.
acts.sub.122:8.6: The visit of the priests from Ur
acts.note.sub:122:8.6.desc: Three priests from Ur in Mesopotamia had heard that the light of life would appear on earth as a babe among the Jews, and they went in search of him. After weeks of futile searching in Jerusalem, Zacharias sent them to Bethlehem, where they found the babe, almost three weeks old, and left their gifts with Mary.
acts.note.sub:122:8.6.diff: The Gospel of Matthew says Magi from the East followed a star and inquired of Herod, whereas The Urantia Book says three priests from Ur came after hearing of a teacher's dream, and Zacharias directed them to Bethlehem.
acts.sub.122:8.7: The legend of the star of Bethlehem
acts.note.sub:122:8.7.desc: The wise men from Ur saw no star to guide them to Bethlehem. The legend of the star arose later from natural conjunctions of Jupiter and Saturn in the constellation of Pisces on May 29, September 29, and December 5 of 7 B.C., upon which a succeeding generation built the story of the star and the Magi.
acts.note.sub:122:8.7.diff: The Gospel of Matthew says a star led the Magi and stood over the place where the child was, whereas The Urantia Book says there was no such star and the legend grew from a conjunction of Jupiter and Saturn.
acts.note.122:9.desc: Joseph and Mary went up to the temple in Jerusalem to present their first-born to the priests for redemption and to offer the sacrifice for Mary's purification. Zacharias, by a prearranged signal, pointed Jesus out, and Simeon, a singer, astonished everyone by singing a poem written by Anna, a poetess.
acts.note.122:9.diff: The Gospel of Luke says Simeon, led by the Holy Spirit, took the child in his arms and Anna prophesied, whereas The Urantia Book says Zacharias identified Jesus by a prearranged signal and the song was a poem Anna had written.
acts.note.122:10.desc: Alerted by the priests from Ur and reports of the temple song, Herod searched for the child in vain, and about the middle of October, 6 B.C., he ordered all boy babies under two in Bethlehem killed; sixteen perished. Warned through Zacharias, Joseph and Mary fled the night before to Alexandria, staying two full years.
acts.note.122:10.diff: The Gospel of Matthew says an angel of the Lord warned Joseph in a dream, whereas The Urantia Book says a believer at Herod's court informed Zacharias, and the massacre of sixteen babies came over a year after the birth.
acts.intro.123: Two years in Alexandria and the return home
acts.note.123:0.desc: In Alexandria Joseph worked as a carpenter and then became foreman of workmen on a public building, while Jesus grew up healthy and was given a Greek copy of the Hebrew scriptures. After Herod's death the family sailed to Joppa, arriving late in August, 4 B.C., and early in October Joseph persuaded Mary to leave for Nazareth.
acts.note.123:1.desc: Reaching Nazareth on the fourth day, the family reclaimed the home where Joseph's brother had been living. Jesus, three years and two months old, made friends with a neighbor boy named Jacob. James was born on April 2, 3 B.C., and that summer Joseph built a workshop near the village spring and the caravan lot.
acts.note.123:1.diff: The Gospel of Matthew says they settled in Nazareth to fulfill a prophet's word, and Luke says they returned soon after fulfilling the law, whereas The Urantia Book says they returned after two years in Egypt by Joseph's own judgment.
acts.note.123:2.desc: On February 11, 2 B.C., a Thought Adjuster came to indwell Jesus, though he was no more aware of it than other children are. His sister Miriam was born on July 11, and when Jesus turned five on August 21, he passed by Galilean custom into his father's charge for his education.
acts.map3.head: Galilean Towns Visited with His Father
acts.map3.1.head: Joseph's building work
acts.map3.1.body: For several years after 1 B.C. Joseph did considerable work at Cana, Bethlehem (of Galilee), Magdala, Nain, Sepphoris, Capernaum, and Endor. When James was old enough to help at home, Jesus made frequent trips with his father to these towns, a keen observer storing up knowledge of man and the way he lived.
acts.map3.2.head: Trips to near-by towns
acts.map3.2.body: When work and caravan travel were slack, he went with his father to near-by Cana, Endor, and Nain. He frequently visited Sepphoris, a little over three miles northwest of Nazareth, the capital of Galilee and a residence of Herod Antipas (circles).
acts.map3.3.head: Uncle's farm and Magdala
acts.map3.3.body: In A.D. 5, while traveling with his father, he also frequently visited his uncle's farm and occasionally went over to Magdala to fish with the uncle who made his headquarters near that city.
acts.map3.4.head: The games at Scythopolis
acts.map3.4.body: About the middle of May, A.D. 5, he went with his father on a business trip to Scythopolis (ancient Beth-shean), the chief Greek city of the Decapolis. He insisted on seeing the annual games of the Decapolis cities in the amphitheater and was thrilled with them.
acts.note.123:3.desc: Joseph taught Jesus Greek using the scriptures received in Alexandria. Jesus suffered his first great shock when his father admitted he did not know what caused an earthquake. In the early summer of 1 B.C. Zacharias' family visited, and Jesus first met John; he insisted on talking to his Father in heaven as he would to Joseph.
acts.note.123:4.desc: In January, A.D. 1, a great snowstorm fell on Galilee, and in July Jesus was injured falling down the stone stairs during a sandstorm, an accident that could not have been prevented. Midwayers do not interfere with material accidents except on orders from superiors. His brother Joseph was born on March 16.
acts.note.123:5.desc: At seven, Jesus entered the Nazareth synagogue school in August, learning Hebrew and the law from the chazan, and graduated at thirteen. He talked with caravan travelers in Greek, chose a passage from Isaiah as his birthday text, and on Sabbaths climbed the hills with his father to view Galilee.
acts.note.123:6.desc: In his eighth year Jesus spent one week each month with his fisherman uncle near Magdala or on another uncle's farm, and he took up mathematics and the harp. Simon was born on April 14. Nahor, a rabbi sent at Zacharias' instigation, urged study in Jerusalem, but after talking with his Father in heaven, Jesus chose to stay home.
acts.note.124:1.desc: In A.D. 3 Jesus challenged the chazan's teaching that all images and pictures were idolatrous, and his charcoal drawing of the teacher brought the elders to Joseph. Joseph upheld the second commandment, and Jesus obeyed. In late June he climbed Mount Tabor with his father, and Martha was born on September 13.
acts.note.124:2.desc: On Sabbath, July 5, A.D. 4, walking with his father, Jesus first expressed feelings that revealed his growing awareness of the unusual nature of his mission. He entered the advanced synagogue school and stirred up Nazareth with his questions. He would not fight for his rights, and Jacob, the stone mason's son, defended him.
acts.note.124:3.desc: When Jude was born on June 24, A.D. 5, Mary was gravely ill, and Jesus, not yet eleven, took on a first-born son's responsibilities. In May he visited Scythopolis with his father and saw the Greek games; his suggestion to build an amphitheater at Nazareth brought the only time he ever saw his father angry with him.
acts.note.124:4.desc: At twelve Jesus worked regularly in the home carpenter shop and managed his own earnings, and, not understanding his dual nature, he passed through seasons of uncertainty about his mission. When he called the ritual of touching the doorpost parchment idolatrous, Joseph removed it, and Jesus struggled to reconcile his convictions with loyalty to his parents.
acts.note.124:5.desc: His youngest brother, Amos, was born on January 9, A.D. 7, and about mid-February Jesus became humanly assured that he was destined to perform a mission on earth. On March 20 he graduated from the Nazareth synagogue school as a son of the commandment, but he sensed he would never study in Jerusalem as the elders planned.
acts.note.124:5.diff: The Gospel of Luke says only that his parents went up every year at Passover and took him when he was twelve, whereas The Urantia Book says his graduation as a son of the commandment qualified him for his first Passover.
acts.map4.head: The First Journey up to Jerusalem
acts.map4.1.head: From Nazareth to Jezreel
acts.map4.1.body: Early Monday morning, April 4, A.D. 7, a company of 103 left Nazareth. Journeying south they passed Shunem on the left; at Jezreel they turned east to avoid passing through Samaria.
acts.map4.2.head: Around Mount Gilboa into the Jordan valley
acts.map4.2.body: Rounding the base of Gilboa, they gazed on the Greek city of Scythopolis only from a distance. Going south down the Jordan valley, a little over three hours from opposite Scythopolis, they camped the first night by a bubbling spring.
acts.map4.3.head: Past the Jabbok to Mount Sartaba
acts.map4.3.body: On the second day they passed where the Jabbok flows into the Jordan from the east, and camped the second night near the base of Mount Sartaba, whose summit held the Alexandrian fortress.
acts.map4.4.head: Jericho
acts.map4.4.body: On the third day they passed two villages recently built by Herod and by nightfall reached Jericho, remaining until the morrow. That evening they walked a mile and a half to the site of ancient Jericho.
acts.map4.5.head: By Bethany to Jerusalem
acts.map4.5.body: The fourth day's climb to Jerusalem. At Bethany, on the eastern slopes of Olivet, they stopped at the house of Simon and met Mary, Martha, and Lazarus. From the brow of Olivet Jesus first saw the Holy City and the temple; on Thursday afternoon they entered Jerusalem and lodged at the home of a well-to-do relative of Mary's.
acts.note.124:6.desc: On April 4, A.D. 7, a company of 103 left Nazareth for Jerusalem by the Jordan valley. At Bethany Jesus met Simon's children, Mary, Martha, and Lazarus, beginning a lifelong friendship. On the night before the Passover Sabbath a messenger commissioned by Immanuel told him the hour had come to be about his Father's business.
acts.map5.head: Jerusalem and the Temple
acts.map5.sub: April, A.D. 7, his first Passover  ·  Paper 125
acts.map5.1.head: First visit to the temple
acts.map5.1.body: In Passover week he was consecrated as a son of the law. He was indignant that his mother had to go to the women's gallery. The money-changers and vendors in the court of the gentiles and the slaughter in the priests' court shocked and sickened him. Joseph showed him the “gate beautiful,” and from the upper court they strolled about, viewing the Asmonean palace, the stately home of Herod, and the tower of the Roman guards.
acts.map5.2.head: Passover at Bethany
acts.map5.2.body: Five Nazareth families ate the Passover with the family of Simon of Bethany. On Wednesday of Passover week Jesus went home with Lazarus to spend the night at Bethany.
acts.map5.3.head: Teaching conferences and the holy of holies
acts.map5.3.body: Lazarus took him exploring Jerusalem. Aside from a few visits to the holy of holies to gaze at what was behind the veil, he spent most of his time at the teaching conferences about the temple.
acts.map5.4.head: The party leaves
acts.map5.4.body: On the first day of the week after the festival, the party gathered near the temple and moved on toward Bethany. Absorbed in a discussion of angels, Jesus was left behind; his parents did not discover it until they reached Jericho.
acts.map5.5.head: Between Bethany and the temple
acts.map5.5.body: After the afternoon discussions he stayed the night in Simon's house at Bethany. Early next day he paused and wept on the brow of Olivet, then joined the temple discussions, and again spent the night at Bethany. The following morning he went to the temple without pausing (dashed: the way back).
acts.map5.6.head: His parents come back to search
acts.map5.6.body: At dawn the next day his parents retraced their steps to Jerusalem and searched all day, first at their relatives' house. On the third day, stopping at the temple on the way to the home of Zacharias, they found him seated among the teachers, after searching more than three days.
acts.map5.7.head: Home
acts.map5.7.body: In silence they set out, arriving at Jericho for the night. Only once did they pause, on the brow of Olivet, where he cried out over Jerusalem. It was a three days' journey to Nazareth.
acts.note.125:0.desc: Jesus refused to go unless his mother came, so Mary went up as well. At the temple he resented the separation of his mother into the women's gallery and was disappointed by the perfunctory consecration rites. He told Joseph that the Father in heaven could not regard his erring children with wrath.
acts.note.125:1.desc: In the court of the gentiles Jesus was shocked by the clamor of the money-changers and merchants and outraged by courtesans parading in the temple precincts. Sickened by the slaughter and blood in the priests' court, he begged his father to take him away, and Joseph led him to the gate beautiful and explained the feasts.
acts.note.125:2.desc: Five Nazareth families kept the Passover at the home of Simon of Bethany, where Jesus related the origin of the Passover. He began to contemplate a Passover without bloodshed, and throughout the week he listened to the temple discussions among the new sons of the commandment and talked with more than one hundred and fifty youths.
acts.note.125:3.desc: On the first day of the week after Passover, the Nazareth party set out, men and women traveling in separate groups. Jesus, absorbed in a temple discussion about angels, was left behind; Mary assumed he was with the men and Joseph that he was with the women, so they did not miss him until they reached Jericho.
acts.note.125:3.diff: The Gospel of Luke says only that the parents supposed he was in the company, whereas The Urantia Book explains that men and women traveled separately, each parent assuming he was with the other, while Jesus was absorbed in a discussion of angels.
acts.note.125:4.desc: Jesus listened to the afternoon discussions and spent the night at Simon's house in Bethany. The next day, on the brow of Olivet, he wept over the people, then boldly joined the discussions with questions. Asked his age, he answered thirteen less four months, but it was ruled that he might continue in the discussions.
acts.note.125:4.diff: The Gospel of Luke says Jesus was twelve years old, whereas The Urantia Book says he lacked a little more than four months of thirteen and had been graduated technically early at Nazareth and consecrated at the Passover.
acts.sub.125:4.2: Joseph and Mary turn back to Jerusalem
acts.note.sub:125:4.2.desc: While Jesus wept over the people on the brow of Olivet early that morning and went on to the temple, Joseph and Mary rose at dawn to retrace their steps to Jerusalem. They first went to the relatives with whom they had lodged during Passover week, but no one had seen him; after searching all day, they returned there for the night.
acts.note.sub:125:4.2.diff: The Gospel of Luke says only that the parents returned to Jerusalem seeking him, whereas The Urantia Book says they first searched their relatives' house while Jesus was spending his nights at Simon's home in Bethany.
acts.note.125:5.desc: On the third day many spectators gathered as Jesus questioned the teachers for more than four hours. He asked what really exists in the holy of holies, why mothers are segregated, why animals are slaughtered, whether trade in the temple is right, and whether the Messiah is to be a temporal prince. His parents passed through the temple several times without finding him.
acts.note.125:6.desc: On the fourth day the leader seated Jesus beside him to state his views on prayer and worship, and his parents, stopping at the temple on their way to Zacharias' home, recognized his voice. When Mary reproached him, he said it was time to be about his Father's business, and on Olivet, on the way home, he cried out over Jerusalem.
acts.note.125:6.diff: The Gospel of Luke says the parents found him in the temple after three days, whereas The Urantia Book says they found him on the fourth day by chance while heading to Zacharias' home, and that he lamented over Jerusalem on the way back.
acts.note.126:0.desc: The fourteenth and fifteenth years were the most crucial of Jesus' earth life. After returning from Jerusalem he spent more time with his father, while his parents failed to understand him. Nazareth praised his exploits among the temple's wise men and expected him to become a great teacher.
acts.note.126:1.desc: In A.D. 8 Jesus became a skilled yoke maker and carpenter, and in summer he climbed the hill where Simeon's tomb stood to pray, looking out over Megiddo, Taanach, and Dothan. Joseph set aside funds for his Jerusalem studies, but his parents began to doubt the destiny of a son who worked no miracles.
acts.note.126:2.desc: On September 25, A.D. 8, Joseph was fatally injured by a falling derrick while working on the governor's residence in Sepphoris and died before Mary reached him. Jesus, just past fourteen, became head of the family, caring for his widowed mother, seven siblings, and a child yet unborn, and his plans to study in Jerusalem collapsed.
acts.note.126:3.desc: Ruth, the youngest child, was born on April 17, A.D. 9. In October Jesus wrote with charcoal on a cedar board a family prayer that later became the Lord's Prayer. Reading the Book of Enoch in the synagogue library, he decided to adopt the title Son of Man, and he became certain he was not the Jewish Messiah.
acts.note.126:4.desc: On the first Sabbath after his fifteenth birthday, arranged by the chazan, Jesus conducted the morning service in the Nazareth synagogue, weaving together passages from Isaiah, Amos, Micah, and other prophets. The people marveled at his solemn and authoritative bearing, and that afternoon he wrote the Ten Commandments in Greek on two boards.
acts.note.126:5.desc: The family lived ever more simply, and by working early and late Jesus earned only about twenty-five cents a day. To keep it from the tax collectors he gave his Greek scriptures to the synagogue, and when Herod ruled that nothing was due Joseph for his work, Jesus never again trusted Herod Antipas.
acts.note.127:1.desc: In A.D. 10, at sixteen, Jesus attained his full physical growth and combined the qualities of a sympathetic friend with those of an authoritative teacher. Another house had to be sold, and James took charge of teaching his three sisters at home. He all but decided to begin his public work only after rearing his family.
acts.note.127:2.desc: In A.D. 11 nationalist organizers came to Nazareth, but Jesus refused to join. His mother, his uncle, and even James urged him, and Isaac, a wealthy moneylender, offered to support the family, yet Jesus cited his duty to his family, declaring that money cannot love, and a speech by James eased the crisis.
acts.map7.head: The Passover with James
acts.map7.1.head: Through Samaria to Jerusalem
acts.map7.1.body: In A.D. 12, with the financial pressure eased, Jesus took his brother James to the Passover. They went up a day early, walking by way of Samaria. He did much thinking at Bethel and when drinking from Jacob's well, and they discussed the traditions of Abraham, Isaac, and Jacob.
acts.map7.2.head: Passover at Bethany
acts.map7.2.body: They ate the Passover supper at Bethany. Simon had been laid to rest, and Jesus, having brought the paschal lamb from the temple, presided as head of the Passover family. After supper he talked with Martha and Lazarus far into the night.
acts.map7.3.head: The temple and the brow of Olivet
acts.map7.3.body: The next day James was received into the commonwealth of Israel at the temple. That morning, viewing the temple from the brow of Olivet, Jesus gazed on Jerusalem in silence. They returned to Bethany for the night (dashed); the next day, at James's insistence, they heard the temple discussions, but Jesus asked no questions.
acts.map7.4.head: Home by Jericho and the Jordan valley
acts.map7.4.body: The next day they journeyed home by Jericho and the Jordan valley, and he told of his trip over this road at thirteen. Back in Nazareth he began work in the old family repair shop. The route beyond the upper Jordan valley is not given in the text.
acts.note.127:3.desc: In A.D. 12 Jesus took James to the Passover through Samaria and presided at the Passover in Bethany as head of the household; in the temple discussions he asked no questions. In September Elizabeth and John visited, and the cousins agreed not to meet again until their public work. On December 3, Amos died of a high fever.
acts.note.127:4.desc: In A.D. 13 Jesus won his mother over to positive training, urging the children to do good rather than merely forbidding evil. He governed his brothers and sisters fairly and lovingly and became the true head of the household. To pay Jude's school expenses he sold his beloved harp.
acts.note.127:5.desc: Rebecca, eldest daughter of Ezra, a wealthy Nazareth merchant, fell in love with Jesus and declared her feelings at her seventeenth birthday celebration. Jesus kindly explained that his duty to rear his father's family left him not free to marry. Heartbroken, Rebecca moved to Sepphoris but waited for him and followed him all her life.
acts.map8.head: The Third Passover Visit to Jerusalem
acts.map8.1.head: From Nazareth to Jerusalem
acts.map8.1.body: He went up by way of Megiddo, Antipatris, and Lydda, spending four days and in part covering the route traveled on the return from Egypt. At Megiddo he thought much about the past events of that battlefield.
acts.map8.2.head: Bethany, the home of Lazarus
acts.map8.2.body: Passing through Jerusalem, he paused only to look upon the temple and went on to Bethany. With Lazarus, Martha, and Mary he shared the first Passover without the paschal lamb, with unleavened bread and wine.
acts.map8.3.head: Back to Nazareth
acts.map8.3.body: On returning home he told all this to his mother. The return route is not given in the text (dashed).
acts.note.127:6.desc: In A.D. 14 Jesus went up to Passover by way of Megiddo and Lydda and at Bethany, with Lazarus, Martha, and Mary, celebrated the first Passover without the paschal lamb, using unleavened bread and wine. He postponed all thought of marriage until his hour should come and stood at the threshold of full manhood.
acts.map9.head: The Fourth Passover Visit — with His Brother Joseph
acts.map9.1.head: By the Jordan valley to Jerusalem
acts.map9.1.body: Having taken James to the temple for consecration, he deemed it his duty to take Joseph. They went by the usual Jordan valley route, and going down the Jordan, Jesus narrated Jewish history to Joseph.
acts.map9.2.head: Passover at Bethany
acts.map9.2.body: As was his custom when in Jerusalem, he spent the Passover with his three friends at Bethany. To most of Joseph's questions he would only reply, “My hour has not yet come.”
acts.map9.3.head: By the east Jordan way through Amathus
acts.map9.3.body: They returned by the road east of the river, and he told Joseph about the reputed tribes of Ruben, Gad, and Gilead that traditionally had dwelt in these regions.
acts.note.128:1.desc: Having reached adulthood, Jesus, fully aware of his dual nature, set about in earnest experiencing the life of the lowest intelligent creature. Until his baptism he used no supernatural power. This year he took Joseph up to Jerusalem for the Passover, going down the Jordan valley and returning by the east Jordan way.
acts.note.128:2.desc: This year Simon went to work with Jacob the stone mason, and Jesus spent six months at Sepphoris learning the smith's trade. Before leaving he formally installed James, just past eighteen, as acting head of the family, beginning to wean the family gradually from dependence on himself.
acts.map10.head: The Fifth Passover Visit — with His Brother Simon
acts.map10.1.head: Through the Decapolis to Jerusalem
acts.map10.1.body: A.D. 17. Jesus stopped work for three weeks to take Simon to Jerusalem for the Passover. They went up by way of Pella, Gerasa, Philadelphia, Heshbon, and Jericho.
acts.map10.2.head: Jerusalem
acts.map10.2.body: A merchant from Damascus whom they met at Philadelphia insisted they stop with him at his Jerusalem headquarters. Simon was received into the commonwealth of Israel at the Passover consecration, and near the Asmonean palace Jesus met a young Hellenist named Stephen and talked with him for four hours.
acts.map10.3.head: Home by the coast route
acts.map10.3.body: Leaving on the Sunday after Passover week, they touched Lydda, Joppa, and Caesarea, went around Mount Carmel to Ptolemais, and arrived home Thursday noon.
acts.note.128:3.desc: Jesus took Simon to the Passover in Jerusalem by way of the Decapolis and returned by the coast route. At Philadelphia he met a merchant from Damascus, and in Jerusalem he talked for four hours with a young Hellenist named Stephen about the way of life and the true God.
acts.note.128:4.desc: Jesus spent the last four months of the year in Damascus as the merchant's guest. The merchant and his backers asked him to head a school of religious philosophy meant to outrival Alexandria, but Jesus declined, knowing that his mission must not be supported by institutions of learning.
acts.note.128:5.desc: In mid-June at Caesarea, five prominent Jews of Alexandria asked Jesus to become a religious teacher in their city, but he replied that his hour had not yet come and refused the purse they offered. In December he consented to the marriage of James and Esta two years later.
acts.map11.head: The Sixth Passover Visit — with His Brother Jude
acts.map11.1.head: By the Jordan valley to Jerusalem
acts.map11.1.body: A.D. 19. Jesus accompanied Jude, who had just graduated from the synagogue school, on his first visit to the temple. Fearing trouble if he took his young brother through Samaria, he went and returned by the Jordan valley.
acts.map11.2.head: Jerusalem: arrest and the military prison
acts.map11.2.body: On the way to the temple they met Lazarus of Bethany. When a Roman guard made improper remarks about a passing Jewish girl, Jude's outburst led to his arrest, and he was taken to the military prison with Jesus by his side. The morning following their second day in prison, Jesus appeared before the military magistrate in Jude's behalf, and they were released.
acts.map11.3.head: A night at Bethany, then Nazareth
acts.map11.3.body: They walked over to Bethany for the night, explaining why they had failed to keep the Passover supper, and set out for Nazareth the following day. This was the last Passover Jesus attended with any member of his family.
acts.note.128:6.desc: With the family debts paid, Jesus took Jude to the Passover in Jerusalem. When Jude denounced a Roman guard and was arrested, Jesus stayed with him in prison and pleaded his case before the military magistrate, who released him. This was the last Passover Jesus attended with any member of his family.
acts.note.128:7.desc: Jesus became strongly conscious of his potential power but resolved to remain subject to his Father's will. In November a double wedding united James and Esta and Miriam and Jacob, and the next day Jesus gave James the repair shop, installed him as head of the household, and prepared to leave home.
acts.map12.head: Zebedee's Boatshop and Jerusalem
acts.map12.1.head: From Nazareth to Tiberias
acts.map12.1.body: A rainy Sunday morning in January, A.D. 21. Explaining only that he was going over to Tiberias and then to other cities about the Sea of Galilee, he took leave of his family. He spent one week at the new city of Tiberias but found little to interest him.
acts.map12.2.head: By Magdala and Bethsaida to Capernaum
acts.map12.2.body: He called on his father's friend Zebedee, the boatbuilder, and joined him in his enterprise, building a new style of boat for a little more than a year. The boatbuilding shops were on the lake to the south of Capernaum; Zebedee's home, where Jesus lived, was near Bethsaida.
acts.map12.3.head: Martha's wedding
acts.map12.3.body: In October of that year he returned to Nazareth to attend Martha's wedding. The route is not given in the text (dashed).
acts.map12.4.head: To Jerusalem
acts.map12.4.body: In March, A.D. 22, he took leave of Zebedee and Capernaum for Jerusalem. For almost two months he listened to the temple discussions, spending most Sabbaths at Bethany. He celebrated the Passover with Zebedee's family, who had come up, at the home of Annas. The route is not given in the text (dashed).
acts.note.129:1.desc: In January, A.D. 21, Jesus left his family and went to Capernaum, where for a little more than a year he built boats with Zebedee, creating a new style of boat and new methods of building. He lived in Zebedee's home, studied in the synagogue, and among the workers was first called the Master.
acts.note.129:2.desc: In March, A.D. 22, Jesus entrusted the monthly money for his family to John Zebedee and went to Jerusalem, where Annas showed him the academies. During Passover week he met a wealthy traveler from India and his son, and agreed, with a year's wages paid in advance, to accompany them as interpreter and tutor.
acts.note.129:3.desc: Jesus spent his whole twenty-ninth year on the Mediterranean tour, known as the Damascus scribe. Only Zebedee knew the facts of this journey. He met and loved all kinds of men, and by its end he virtually knew that he was a Son of God.
acts.note.129:4.desc: During this period the purely human religious experience of the Son of Man well-nigh reached its apex. He lived the mortal life from beginning to end, through joy and sorrow, becoming not a pattern to copy but a new and living way by which others may live their own lives by the same means.
acts.intro.130: The beginning of the two-year tour to Rome
acts.map13.head: The Journey to Rome, Greece, and Mesopotamia
acts.map13.1.head: Jerusalem to Caesarea by way of Joppa
acts.map13.1.body: Sunday morning, April 26, A.D. 22, with Gonod and his son Ganid from India. At Joppa he met Gadiah, a Philistine interpreter; at Caesarea he helped make a new steering paddle for the ship.
acts.map13.2.head: To Alexandria
acts.map13.2.body: When the boat was ready, they departed at noon one day for Alexandria in Egypt.
acts.map13.3.head: To Lasea in Crete
acts.map13.3.body: They walked about the island and climbed the mountains.
acts.map13.4.head: By Cyrene to Carthage
acts.map13.4.body: Two days at Cyrene, where they gave first aid to an injured lad named Rufus.
acts.map13.5.head: By Malta, Syracuse, and Messina to Naples
acts.map13.5.body: At Malta a long talk with a young man named Claudus; a full week at Syracuse; one day at Messina.
acts.map13.6.head: By Capua and the Appian Way to Rome
acts.map13.6.body: Three days at Capua. On the third day after arriving in Rome they appeared before Tiberius. They made five trips from Rome, one to the northern Italian lakes (thin dashes).
acts.map13.7.head: On foot by the Appian Way to Tarentum
acts.map13.7.body: Their belongings went ahead by pack train to Tarentum, while the three walked leisurely across Italy.
acts.map13.8.head: By Nicopolis and Corinth to Athens
acts.map13.8.body: Several days at Nicopolis; at Corinth they met Crispus, the chief ruler of the synagogue.
acts.map13.9.head: By Troas to Ephesus
acts.map13.9.body: From Athens by way of Troas to Ephesus, the capital of the Roman province of Asia.
acts.map13.10.head: By Rhodes and Cyprus to Antioch
acts.map13.10.body: Stopping at Rhodes, they sailed for Cyprus, landed at Paphos and rested in the near-by mountains, then embarked at Salamis for Antioch in Syria.
acts.map13.11.head: By Sidon to Damascus
acts.map13.11.body: After preparing their luggage for the camel caravan, they went down to Sidon and thence over to Damascus.
acts.map13.12.head: By caravan to Mesopotamia
acts.map13.12.body: Through Thapsacus and Larissa to Babylon; they visited Ur and other places and went by Susa to Charax. On December 10, A.D. 23, at Charax on the Persian Gulf, he said good-bye to Gonod and Ganid.
acts.map13.13.head: The return
acts.map13.13.body: By way of Ur he went back to Babylon and joined a desert caravan bound for Damascus. From Damascus he went to Nazareth, stopping only a few hours at Capernaum to call on Zebedee's family (dashed).
acts.note.130:0.desc: On April 26, A.D. 22, Jesus left Jerusalem with Gonod and his son Ganid from India, traveling by Joppa, Caesarea, Alexandria, Carthage, Rome, Corinth, Ephesus, and many other places, until he parted from them at Charax on December 10, A.D. 23. Jesus taught Ganid and served as Gonod's interpreter.
acts.note.130:1.desc: At Joppa Jesus met Gadiah, a Philistine interpreter working for Simon the tanner. When Gadiah asked about Jonah and the big fish, Jesus answered by warning against running away from duty. On good and evil he taught that God does not create evil; evil results from immature choosing.
acts.note.130:2.desc: While a broken steering paddle was replaced, Jesus stayed in Caesarea, talking with a merchant from Mongolia and urging a young Greek, Anaxand, to overcome his unjust foreman with goodness. He explained to Ganid the difference between God's will and man's will, and that a dog has no spiritual nature.
acts.note.130:3.desc: In Alexandria Jesus and Ganid saw the lighthouse on Pharos and spent time daily in the world's greatest library and museum. Under Jesus' direction Ganid began collecting the teachings of world religions that recognized a Universal Deity. They did not meet Philo, who was ill.
acts.note.130:4.desc: The night before leaving Alexandria, after meeting a professor who lectured on Plato, Jesus explained to Ganid the nature of universe reality. The source of reality is the Infinite; personality retains its identity amid change; and evil is the shadow of imperfection cast by a finite universe.
acts.note.130:5.desc: On Crete the travelers rested and climbed the mountains, and Jesus had his first long talk about religion with Gonod. When Ganid asked why he did not teach publicly, Jesus said everything must await its time. At Fair Havens he rescued a slave girl being beaten by a drunken man.
acts.note.130:6.desc: In the mountains of Crete Jesus approached a fearful, downcast young man named Fortune by asking the way to Phenix, then urged him to be reborn as a man of faith, courage, and service. At Cyrene Jesus and Ganid gave first aid to Rufus, son of Simon, injured in an oxcart accident.
acts.note.130:7.desc: On the way to Carthage Jesus talked mostly of social and political matters, and when Ganid asked how to make friends, he said to take a genuine interest in one's fellows. At Carthage he held a long talk with a Mithraic priest about immortality, time, and space.
acts.note.130:8.desc: At Malta Jesus helped Claudus, a young man who had contemplated taking his life, and at Syracuse he helped Ezra, a backslidden Jew, find God. At Messina he encouraged a boy fruit vendor, and then by way of Naples and Capua the party traveled the Appian Way to Rome.
acts.note.131:0.desc: At Alexandria Ganid employed more than sixty translators to collect what the world's religions taught about God's relation to man. Most of these monotheistic teachings derived from the Melchizedek missionaries, and he arranged them under ten headings.
acts.note.131:1.desc: Ganid chose passages from Cynic writings, which best preserved Melchizedek's teachings. They declare that God is supreme, the Most High of heaven and earth, merciful and everywhere present, and that the man who knows God regards all men as his brethren and overcomes evil with good.
acts.note.131:2.desc: From records preserved by the Kenites and modified by the Jews, Jesus and Ganid selected passages declaring God to be the one Lord who created heaven and earth, a merciful and righteous shepherd. The command to love your neighbor as yourself and the Ten Commandments were included.
acts.note.131:3.desc: Ganid was shocked to find how near Buddhism came to being a great religion without a personal God. The passages he chose teach that faith brings peace and virtue, that evil is the fruit of wrong thinking, that deeds bring sure reward, and that one should conquer self and overcome evil with good.
acts.note.131:4.desc: The monotheistic doctrine of the Melchizedek missionaries was embodied in the later teachings of Hinduism. Jesus and Ganid extracted passages declaring God to be the one creator and controller of the universe of universes, who dwells in the human soul, and that knowing him breaks the bonds of death.
acts.note.131:5.desc: Zoroaster was in contact with descendants of the Melchizedek missionaries, and next to Judaism his religion preserved the most of the Salem teachings. Ganid chose passages teaching that all things come from the One God of light, all-wise and good, that repentance and forgiveness remove sin, and that the righteous attain immortality.
acts.note.131:6.desc: The third group in India preserving Melchizedek's teaching of one God was known in those days as the Suduanists, the Jains. They taught that the Lord of Heaven is supreme and that man's greatest victory is the conquest of self, which shows itself in anger, pride, deceit, and greed.
acts.note.131:7.desc: Records of Shinto, a Far-Eastern religion, had only recently been lodged in the Alexandrian library and also showed traces of Melchizedek's teaching. They say the Lord, creator of heaven and earth, values even the prayer of the poorest, and that pride obscures God, so one must come to him with a pure heart.
acts.note.131:8.desc: Of the Melchizedek messengers' teaching of one God in China, the most survived in Taoism. Ganid's passages say the Supreme One is the honored ancestor of all things, nourishing creatures without coercion; true goodness is like water; and good should be done without thought of reward.
acts.note.131:9.desc: Even Confucianism, the least God-recognizing of the great religions, bore traces of monotheism. Ganid's summary says that what Heaven appoints is without error, that benevolence is Heaven's greatest gift, that faults should be promptly confessed and corrected, and that one should not do to others what one does not wish for oneself.
acts.note.131:10.desc: Ganid set down the faith he had reached through Jesus' teaching, calling it our religion. It confesses one God, the Father in heaven, whose spirit dwells in man; since all men are brothers, he resolves to do to others as he would have them do to him and to love even his enemies.
acts.note.132:0.desc: On their third day in Rome, Jesus and the two Indians appeared before the Emperor Tiberius. For almost six months Jesus personally taught thirty-two leaders of the Stoics, Cynics, and mystery cults, never attacking their errors but selecting and illuminating the truth in their teachings; thirty of them later helped lay the foundation of Christianity in Rome.
acts.note.132:1.desc: Jesus talked all night with Angamon, leader of the Stoics in Rome. He taught that the standard of true values must be sought in the spiritual world, that materialistic progress without moral insight endangers civilization, and that scientists and religionists should serve human progress rather than fight each other.
acts.note.132:2.desc: Answering Mardus, leader of the Cynics of Rome, Jesus said good and evil represent relative levels of human comprehension of the universe. Goodness is always a growing, personal experience, and while the possibility of evil is necessary to moral choosing, actual evil is not.
acts.note.132:3.desc: Nabon, high priest of the Mithraic cult, sought to convert Jesus but was instead deeply impressed by his teaching on truth and faith. Jesus said truth can be defined only by living; knowledge deals with facts, wisdom with relationships, and truth with reality values, and truth cannot be possessed without faith.
acts.note.132:4.desc: In Rome Jesus personally ministered to more than five hundred people of every class, telling them of the heavenly Father's love. He talked with a senator, with the slaveholder Claudius, with a Greek physician, and with an orator, and he defended a falsely accused poor man before a magistrate, winning his release.
acts.note.132:5.desc: When a rich Roman introduced by Angamon asked what to do with his wealth, Jesus divided riches into ten sources, including inherited, discovered, trade, interest, and earned wealth, and counseled him to administer each with justice and fairness, restoring anything unfairly gained. The rich man promised to follow this counsel.
acts.note.132:6.desc: In Rome Jesus and Ganid spent hours restoring a lost child to his mother and helped a widow with five children, whose husband had died in an accident, by finding work for her eldest son. When Gonod urged him to write a book, Jesus replied that his mission was to live a life.
acts.note.132:7.desc: On trips around Rome, Jesus explained to Ganid that God cannot be revealed to a man who is not hungry for truth. In the Swiss mountains he told Gonod that Buddha was an orphan prophet who lost sight of God, and when Ganid proposed making a new religion, Jesus answered that religion is not made.
acts.note.133:0.desc: Jesus left Rome without saying good-bye, and those who had known him later formed small groups. The three travelers walked the Appian Way to Tarentum. On the way Ganid asked about India's caste system, and Jesus answered that before God all mortals stand on an equal footing.
acts.note.133:1.desc: Near Tarentum Jesus rescued a small boy being beaten by a bigger one and held the bully, but he restrained Ganid when the youth began to thrash the offender. He explained that mercy is the work of the individual, while justice punishment belongs to society and government, and they also discussed self-defense.
acts.note.133:2.desc: At the Tarentum landing Jesus took aside a man who was mistreating his wife and kindly counseled him, and the man repented. Jesus told him that to love and cherish his wife as an equal partner is to be like God. The party sailed by way of Nicopolis to Corinth.
acts.note.133:3.desc: At Corinth Jesus held more than twenty sessions with Crispus, the chief ruler of the synagogue. One night, when Ganid rudely drove away two courtesans, Jesus told him not to judge them and brought the women to the home of Justus to help them start a new life. Many met here later joined Paul's church.
acts.note.133:4.desc: At Corinth Jesus gave fitting counsel to many: a miller, a Roman centurion, a Mithraic leader, an Epicurean teacher, a builder, a judge, the mistress of an inn, a Chinese merchant, a traveler from Britain, a runaway lad, and a condemned criminal, each according to his situation.
acts.note.133:5.desc: At their inn in Athens Jesus discussed science with a Greek philosopher. He said science deals with physical energies and religion with eternal values, that logic and mathematics cannot be applied unchanged to the problems of life, and that facts and values are ultimately unified in the Supreme.
acts.note.133:6.desc: At Ephesus the travelers visited the temple of Artemis, and after Ganid bought a little silver shrine, they talked at length about worshiping things made with human hands. When a philosopher asked what the soul is, Jesus answered that it is the truth-discerning and spirit-perceiving part of man, born together with moral activity.
acts.note.133:7.desc: While resting in the mountains of Cyprus, Ganid was suddenly stricken with fever, and Jesus nursed him devotedly. During his convalescence Ganid asked about man's higher self-consciousness, and Jesus explained that self-consciousness is a reality, and that the mind cannot stand double allegiance but is unified by full dedication to the Father's will.
acts.note.133:8.desc: At Antioch Jesus did not go with them to the groves of Daphne, and as the journey's end neared he grew reflective, saying only that he might come back there sometime. Ganid put Jesus' teaching into practice by visiting a disgruntled countryman employed by his father and telling him of the Father in heaven.
acts.note.133:9.desc: From Damascus the travelers crossed the desert by caravan and visited Ur and Susa; at Ur Ganid learned the difference between knowledge, wisdom, and truth. Jesus bade farewell to Gonod and Ganid at Charax, and they never learned that their teacher Joshua was the later Jesus of Nazareth.
acts.note.134:0.desc: After the Mediterranean tour Jesus gave final approval to the plan of being born in Palestine of Jewish parents. He decided to return to Galilee and await the beginning of his work as a public teacher, and to finish his life among the Jews of Palestine, where it had begun.
acts.map14.head: Lake Urmia and the Caravan Trip to the Caspian Sea
acts.map14.1.head: The caravan trip to the Caspian Sea
acts.map14.1.body: Jesus left Nazareth on April 1, A.D. 24, as conductor of a large caravan, taking the place of its conductor, who had been taken violently ill. Going from Jerusalem, the caravan went by way of Damascus and Lake Urmia through Assyria, Media, and Parthia to the southeastern Caspian Sea region. It was a full year before he returned.
acts.map14.2.head: Urmia
acts.map14.2.body: On the way out he stopped several days for rest at the old Persian city of Urmia on the western shores of Lake Urmia. On an island near by stood the temple of the philosophy of religions built by Cymboyton.
acts.map14.3.head: The return
acts.map14.3.body: He gave up the direction of the caravan at Lake Urmia, tarried slightly over two weeks to give the lectures on "The Brotherhood of Men," and returned as a passenger with a later caravan to Damascus.
acts.map14.4.head: To Capernaum
acts.map14.4.body: At Damascus the owners of the camels besought him to remain in their service. Declining, he journeyed on to Capernaum, arriving April 1, A.D. 25. Capernaum, not Nazareth, was now his home; there he made his home with the Zebedees.
acts.note.134:1.desc: Returning from Charax in December, A.D. 23, Jesus turned over to James the little house in Capernaum that John Zebedee had bought, then spent several weeks in Nazareth. Simon and Jude were married at a double wedding in early March, A.D. 24, and after Jesus left as a caravan conductor, Mary and Ruth moved to the Capernaum home.
acts.map15.head: Syria and the Mediterranean Coast
acts.map15.1.head: Capernaum to Nazareth
acts.map15.1.body: Back from the journey to the Caspian Sea on April 1, A.D. 25, he made a brief visit to Capernaum and went on to Nazareth, stopping over a few days. Only one more trip outside of Palestine remained, and that was into Syria.
acts.map15.2.head: By Tyre and Sidon to Antioch
acts.map15.2.body: In the middle of April he left Nazareth for Tyre. From there he journeyed on north, tarrying for a few days at Sidon, but his destination was Antioch.
acts.map15.3.head: Antioch
acts.map15.3.body: He lived here for over two months, working, observing, studying, visiting, and ministering; for three weeks he worked as a tentmaker. He remained longer in Antioch than at any other place he visited on this trip. This year he was known by various names, among them the scribe of Damascus.
acts.map15.4.head: Along the coast to Caesarea and Joppa
acts.map15.4.body: From Antioch he journeyed south along the coast to Caesarea, where he tarried for a few weeks, continuing down the coast to Joppa.
acts.note.134:2.desc: On April 1, A.D. 24, Jesus took the place of a caravan conductor who had fallen ill and led the caravan by way of Damascus and Lake Urmia to the southeastern Caspian Sea region. He contacted every surviving race except the red, and returned to Capernaum on April 1, A.D. 25, making his home with the Zebedees.
acts.note.134:3.desc: On the way to the Caspian, Jesus took part in discussions at the temple of religious philosophy built by Cymboyton at Urmia. On the return trip he stayed two weeks and delivered twenty-four lectures on the brotherhood of men, the most systematic and formal of all his teachings.
acts.note.134:4.desc: The Urmia lectures taught that the brotherhood of men is founded on the fatherhood of God and that the kingdom of heaven is the spiritual relation between God and man. Religious peace can come only when all religions surrender ecclesiastical authority and notions of religious sovereignty and recognize God alone as spirit sovereign.
acts.note.134:5.desc: Restated by the midwayers for modern conditions, this teaching holds that war will never end while nations cling to unlimited national sovereignty. As sovereignty evolves from the family toward all mankind, lasting peace will come only when nations surrender the power to make war to a representative government of mankind.
acts.note.134:6.desc: The teaching holds that liberty is a gift of civilization made possible by the enforcement of law, and that war is not the disease but a symptom of the virus of national sovereignty. After Cymboyton's death, intolerant teachers sent by Abner increased the confusion, and the school closed after five years.
acts.map16.head: Through Palestine to Mount Hermon
acts.map16.1.head: Joppa to Beersheba
acts.map16.1.body: From Joppa he traveled inland to Jamnia, Ashdod, and Gaza. From Gaza he took the inland trail to Beersheba, where he remained for a week.
acts.map16.2.head: North from Beersheba
acts.map16.2.body: His final tour, as a private individual, through the heart of Palestine. He stopped at Hebron, Bethlehem (where he saw his birthplace), Jerusalem (he did not visit Bethany), Beeroth, Lebonah, Sychar, Schecham, Samaria, Geba, En-Gannim, Endor, and Madon.
acts.map16.3.head: To Caesarea-Philippi
acts.map16.3.body: Passing through Magdala and Capernaum, he journeyed on north; passing east of the Waters of Merom, he went by Karahta to Dan, or Caesarea-Philippi. Karahta is not marked, as its location is unknown.
acts.map16.4.head: Six weeks on Mount Hermon
acts.map16.4.body: He made ready his supplies and, with a lad named Tiglath, proceeded along the Damascus road to Beit Jenn in the foothills of Mount Hermon. Near the middle of August, A.D. 25, he established his headquarters there and ascended the lonely slopes of the mountain, living alone with God for six weeks (the dotted line ends on the mountain; position approximate).
acts.note.134:7.desc: Back from the Caspian, Jesus left Nazareth in mid-April, A.D. 25, for Tyre and Sidon and lived over two months in Antioch. He then went down the coast to Gaza and Beersheba, and from Beersheba to Dan made his final tour through Palestine as a private individual.
acts.map17.head: From Mount Hermon to Jerusalem, and Back to Galilee
acts.map17.sub: Late summer, A.D. 25 – January, A.D. 26  ·  Paper 134
acts.map17.1.head: Mount Hermon to Capernaum
acts.map17.1.body: Coming down the mountain, he met Tiglath coming up with food and turned him back. At Dan he took leave of the lad, giving him the donkey, and proceeded south by the same way he had come, to Capernaum.
acts.map17.2.head: With John to Jerusalem
acts.map17.2.body: After a family meeting in Capernaum over the Sabbath, he started the next day with John the son of Zebedee, going to the east of the lake and by Gerasa and on down the Jordan valley. They stopped overnight at Bethany with Lazarus and his sisters, going early the next morning to Jerusalem.
acts.map17.3.head: Jerusalem and the hills near Bethany
acts.map17.3.body: They spent almost three weeks in and around the city and were present at the services of the day of atonement; then came the feast of tabernacles. In the midst of that week he took leave of John and spent almost a week alone in the hills near Bethany.
acts.map17.4.head: By Gilboa to Capernaum
acts.map17.4.body: On the way home he spent a day and a night alone on the slopes of Gilboa, near where King Saul had taken his life. The morning after reaching Capernaum he presented himself for work in Zebedee's boatshop, and he worked there until January of the following year.
acts.note.134:8.desc: In mid-August, A.D. 25, Jesus left the lad Tiglath at Beit Jenn and spent six weeks alone on Mount Hermon. In the last week Satan and Caligastia appeared and tempted him, but he only answered that the will of his Paradise Father should prevail, and thereby won the sovereignty of Nebadon.
acts.note.134:8.diff: The Gospels place the temptation in the wilderness for forty days right after the baptism, with three tests of bread, temple pinnacle, and kingdoms; The Urantia Book says it occurred on Mount Hermon before the baptism, concerned universe sovereignty, and calls the Gospel account symbolic.
acts.note.134:9.desc: Coming down from Hermon, Jesus went with John Zebedee to Jerusalem for the day of atonement and the feast of tabernacles, but felt the atonement rites misrepresented his Father's character. He then built boats with James in Capernaum until January, A.D. 26, when John the Baptist reached Pella, and saying his hour had come, Jesus went to be baptized.
acts.note.135:0.desc: John the Baptist was born March 25, 7 B.C., in accordance with the promise Gabriel had made to Elizabeth, and was circumcised on the eighth day. He grew up as an ordinary child in the City of Judah, west of Jerusalem, and his parents, the priest Zacharias and Elizabeth, gave him systematic mental and spiritual training.
acts.note.135:0.diff: The Gospel of Luke tells of the naming of John and of Zacharias's tongue being loosed to prophesy, whereas The Urantia Book says that apart from Gabriel's visit and Zacharias's dream nothing supernatural attended John's birth.
acts.note.135:1.desc: At fourteen John went with his parents to Engedi by the Dead Sea, the southern headquarters of the Nazarite brotherhood, where he took the lifelong Nazarite vow and then offered sacrifice at the temple in Jerusalem. At sixteen, inspired by reading about Elijah, he began wearing a hair garment and a leather girdle.
acts.note.135:2.desc: When Zacharias died in July, A.D. 12, John made purification offerings because of his Nazarite vow. That September in Nazareth Jesus admonished him to return home and care for his mother. Since John refused the priestly allowance, money grew scarce, so he and Elizabeth moved to Hebron, and he visited Engedi more and more often.
acts.note.135:3.desc: John built stone shelters along a valley brook and herded sheep with Ezda, an orphan lad of Beth-zur, living on mutton, goat's milk, wild honey, and locusts. A great lover of the Prophet Daniel, he grew convinced that the old order was ending and the kingdom of heaven drawing near, while his mother assured him that Jesus was the Messiah.
acts.note.135:4.desc: After Elizabeth died on August 17, A.D. 22, John gave his flocks to the brotherhood and stayed two and a half years at Engedi, reading Isaiah and Malachi. Long troubled by the prophecy that Elijah must come first, he finally resolved to be the herald of the Messiah and left Engedi in March, A.D. 25.
acts.note.135:5.desc: When John appeared, the Jews, shaped by the apocalyptists, believed the kingdom of heaven was near. Their hopes varied widely: an earthly kingdom under a son of David, a new heaven and a new earth, a Son of Man coming from heaven. Thus John's announcement of the kingdom carried no fewer than half a dozen meanings.
acts.note.135:6.desc: Early in March, A.D. 25, John began preaching at Bethany ford, opposite Jericho, baptizing Jews for the remission of sins. For four months tens of thousands came to hear him. He demanded fruits worthy of repentance from Pharisees and Sadducees and gave practical counsel to publicans and soldiers.
acts.note.135:6.diff: The Gospels speak of camel's hair and locusts with wild honey; The Urantia Book describes a hair garment and explains the stones as the twelve memorial stones Joshua set up. It places the words about the coming one in the later northern journey.
acts.sub.135:6.6: Priests and Levites ask whether John is the Messiah
acts.note.sub:135:6.6.desc: In May, while John still lingered at Bethany ford, the priests and Levites sent a delegation to ask whether he claimed to be the Messiah and by whose authority he preached. John told them to tell their masters they had heard the voice crying in the wilderness, as spoken by Isaiah.
acts.note.sub:135:6.6.diff: The Gospel of John has him deny being the Christ, Elijah, and the prophet in one exchange, whereas The Urantia Book has him answer only with Isaiah's words here and places the denials with a second delegation at Pella.
acts.note.135:7.desc: John journeyed north up the Jordan, pausing at more than a dozen places. He never doubted the coming kingdom but was unsure whether Jesus would be its ruler. At Adam, when his disciples asked whether he was the Messiah, he first spoke of a greater one coming after him who would baptize with the Holy Spirit.
acts.note.135:7.diff: The Gospels set these words in John's general preaching at the Jordan, whereas The Urantia Book places them first at Adam, answering his disciples' question; Matthew and Luke's mention of baptism with fire is absent.
acts.map18.head: The Baptism near Pella and the Forty Days in the Perean Hills
acts.map18.1.head: Capernaum to the Jordan near Pella
acts.map18.1.body: Just before the noon rest on Sunday, January 13, A.D. 26, he laid down his tools in the boatshop, saying, "My hour has come," and started for Pella with his brothers James and Jude. They tarried for the night in the Jordan valley and arrived on the scene of John's baptizing about noon of the next day.
acts.map18.2.head: Forty days in the Perean hills
acts.map18.2.body: Coming up out of the water, he went toward the hills to the east, and no man saw him again for forty days. He lived in an ancient rock cavern in the side of the hills near a village sometime called Beit Adis and drank from a small spring near this rock shelter.
acts.map18.3.head: Down to Pella
acts.map18.3.body: Early on Saturday morning, February 23, he came down from the hills to rejoin John's company encamped at Pella. He took a lad who had injured himself to his parents in the near-by village of Pella.
acts.note.135:8.desc: On January 13, A.D. 26, Jesus laid down his tools at the Capernaum boatshop and went to Pella with his brothers James and Jude. At noon the next day John baptized the three in the Jordan. The four men in the water saw an apparition over Jesus and heard a voice call him a beloved Son; Jesus then departed for the eastern hills.
acts.note.135:8.diff: The Gospels have Jesus come alone, the heavens open, and the Spirit descend like a dove, whereas The Urantia Book says he was baptized with his two brothers and only the four saw the apparition and heard the voice, with no dove.
acts.note.135:9.desc: During Jesus' forty days in the hills, John preached with new certainty while his disciples debated the Messiah's nature. A Jerusalem deputation came to Pella asking who he was, and on February 23 John proclaimed the returning Jesus the Son of God. The next day the two parted for the last time.
acts.note.135:9.diff: The Gospel of John has Jesus introduced the day after the deputation's questioning, whereas The Urantia Book says the deputation came about three weeks after Jesus left and the proclamation came on February 23, after the forty days.
acts.note.sub:135:9.4.desc: About three weeks after Jesus left, a new deputation from the priests and Pharisees at Jerusalem arrived at Pella and asked John whether he was Elijah, the prophet Moses promised, or the Messiah. He denied each and said that one who had been among them would return and baptize them with the Holy Spirit.
acts.note.sub:135:9.4.diff: The Gospel of John sets this exchange at Bethany beyond the Jordan, whereas The Urantia Book places it with a second deputation at Pella and describes the coming one as having been among them and about to return.
acts.sub.135:9.7: "Behold, the Son of God" — John's proclamation
acts.note.sub:135:9.7.desc: Early on the Sabbath, February 23, as Jesus approached from the north, John stood on a large rock and proclaimed him the Son of God, the deliverer of the world. He called him the one who came after him yet was before him, and testified that he had seen the divine spirit descend upon him and heard God's voice.
acts.note.sub:135:9.7.diff: The Gospel of John calls him the Lamb of God who takes away the sin of the world and says John did not know him, whereas The Urantia Book has "the Son of God, the deliverer of the world" and no dove.
acts.note.135:10.desc: On March 3, A.D. 26, John and his remaining disciples turned south, while about a quarter of his followers went to Galilee in search of Jesus. Near Adam John attacked Herod Antipas for taking another man's wife. Back at Bethany ford by June, he was seized by Herod's agents early on June 12.
acts.note.135:11.desc: John languished in prison for more than a year and a half, often tempted to doubt Jesus' mission. Months into his imprisonment he told his disciples that Jesus must increase while he must decrease. A few days before his death he sent messengers asking if Jesus was the Messiah, and received the Master's last word.
acts.note.135:11.diff: The Gospel of Matthew says John was imprisoned for rebuking Herod over Herodias, his brother Philip's wife, whereas The Urantia Book gives both Herod's fear of rebellion and his resentment at John's criticism of his marital affairs.
acts.note.sub:135:11.2.desc: Several months into his imprisonment, John's disciples complained that Jesus feasted with publicans and sinners yet did nothing to free him. John replied that he was not the Messiah but one sent before to prepare the way, rejoicing as the bridegroom's friend: he must increase, but I must decrease.
acts.note.sub:135:11.2.diff: The Gospel of John records these words while John was still baptizing, after a dispute about purification, whereas The Urantia Book places them in prison several months after his arrest.
acts.note.sub:135:11.3–4.desc: Realizing he had uttered a prophecy, John never again wholly doubted Jesus, yet was sorely disappointed that Jesus did not free him. Days before his death he sent two disciples to ask if Jesus was the Messiah. Jesus replied that he had not forgotten John and that the poor have good tidings preached to them; this was John's last word from him.
acts.note.sub:135:11.3–4.diff: The Gospels have Jesus cite the blind seeing and the dead raised and then praise John to the crowd, whereas The Urantia Book's answer lists no miracles and carries the comfort that John is not forgotten.
acts.note.135:12.desc: John was held in the prison of the fortress of Machaerus. Herod feared rebellion if he released him and riot if he killed him. At a birthday feast in the Machaerian palace, the drunken Herod promised Herodias's daughter whatever she asked; at her mother's bidding she requested John's head, and he was beheaded that night.
acts.note.135:12.diff: The Gospels do not name the place, whereas The Urantia Book identifies the fortress and palace of Machaerus in Perea and adds that Herod made his promise while heavy with wine; otherwise the story is much the same.
